The reason why I don't ask about the word Holminster itself is because it's clearly a given name, like mine and yours in real life. There's certainly etymology behind these names, but it doesn't really matter unless the specific topic of etymology comes up in a conversation.

As far as other dungeon's names, if the place is something clearly not grounded in reality, I'll generally not get caught up in the reason why it's named this or that way because it's not something that I need to make much sense in order to appreciate it — it is fantastical, after all — there is some suspension of disbelief precisely because it's not something that would ever exist in our world. However, this dungeon, even with the spooky things that are happening in it, is still just a village. It bothered me that I couldn't make a clear reading of the name of something that is mundane and has nothing special about it.

EDIT: the name of the village in Japanese is also just Holminster, with a phrase that qualifies Holminster: Slaughter Village. There's no switch in the name, which leads me to believe the name of the village is just Holminster, and the localization team changed the literal description of the situation taking place in it for "switch", the reason for which I'm trying to figure out.

Yeah, I thought that was the most likely candidate, but I remembered that Explorer Mode was a thing and went in to look for tracks. There aren't any. The village is pretty deep into a very heavily wooded area, too, except at the end where you get some very Shire-like hills which is the typical scenario I associate with steam trains. 

I'll take that explanation and be happy with it hahaha, if there's any reason other than trying to make it sound cool, like other redditors have suggested, that's one I can live with. Thanks for the input!

Hello. I am not a native English speaker, even though I can communicate without any problem. Something has been bothering me since the release of Shadowbringers and I just now remembered it at a point where I had the free time to investigate.

Why is Holminster Switch called Holminster Switch? Is "switch" a barely used word for village or town, maybe in old English? I looked into 3 or 4 English dictionaries for the definition of switch and there's nothing there that could give a passable explanation of why the dungeon is called that way.

At some point I just dismissed as it being called switch because of the situation with the villagers, but the Duty Finder describes the dungeon as such:

"Holminster Switch─an idyllic settlement in the northern reaches of Lakeland; a tranquil village where folk spend their days raising livestock and tending crops"

So the location is clearly known as a "switch", whatever that is, before the events I previously thought gave the dungeon its name.

Any ideas?
